name: Sara Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good morning, Sara. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be shared with your name. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Millbrook, a pig and maize farm run by Grace Okafor and her brother. I'm in the farrowing house most days, which is where the sows give birth, so I check the piglets, clean the pens and help with injections. In September everyone helps bring in the maize for silage, and I drive the trailer badly. I'm three years in and Grace still double-checks my piglet counts, which is fair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a bank teller for twenty-nine years, and then they closed our branch and put in a machine and an app. I took the package and wanted to do something nobody could put in an app. My husband Marco is an accountant at a small firm in town, and our two are grown, Luca's an engineer and Giulia's a vet nurse. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check a recipe or a word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds familiar. When the bank brought in the app, everybody said the same thing, and it closed us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad it calmed down, and that people shouldn't believe every headline. At the farm gate I'd just say, well, the piglets still need counting. Online I keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd relax. The farrowing house is hands and noses, not screens. Marco's job would be safe too, which is the one I really watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my four days at Millbrook and keep learning the injections properly. Marco and I would keep paying into savings and stick to retiring around sixty-five. Maybe we'd finally book the trip to see my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marco's job is the one you really watch. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his day is spreadsheets and tax forms, and I've seen what happens to desk jobs. When my bank branch closed, the machine that replaced me fit in a wall, so I'll always watch a desk job closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the farm itself has any pressures, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pig prices are up and down, and feed costs went up last year. Grace grumbled, but she's careful. I don't think my job's at risk from that.

say: I'm glad it **calmed down**; don't believe every headline.
At the farm gate: the **piglets** still need counting.
think: The **farrowing house** is hands and noses, not screens.
**Marco's job** would be safe too, and that's the one I watch.
do: Keep my **four days** at Millbrook and learn the piglet injections properly.
S0.quote: When my bank branch closed, the machine that replaced me fit in a wall, so I'll always watch a desk job closely.
fieldNote: Her **bank branch closing** makes her watchful of any desk job.
She tracks **Marco's accounting work** as the family's real exposure.
Farm money pressures exist, but she trusts **Grace's caution**.

steps.text: Keep four days a week in the farrowing house at Millbrook
Keep paying into savings with Marco to retire around sixty-five

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bank all over again, but for Marco this time. Checking, writing, answering customers, that's his whole week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to adapt and not panic, people adjusted before. I'd tell friends to keep an eye on their own jobs. I wouldn't say much about Marco outside the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect his firm to shrink. He's sixty and one of three partners, but the young ones are cheaper and know the software. My job's fine, it's his hours I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Marco and plan for him going down to three days by sixty-two. I'd put more into savings now, while we have two full wages. And I'd learn the farm's new sow records app properly, once Grace has it running, so I'm useful for the screen side too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a low steady kind. I'd notice myself checking the budget more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco say if you suggested three days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's fine, then lie awake. Marco hates change even more than I do. My husband Marco has done the same tax forms for thirty years, and he'd rather lose a finger than a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if his hours dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, probably, since Millbrook's only ten minutes on the bike. Then the weekend meals out. Not the savings, never the savings.

say: It's sensible to **adapt, not panic**, as people did before.
Friends should **watch their own jobs**, but I'd keep Marco's private.
think: Marco's **accounting firm** would likely shrink, and he's sixty.
**My job's fine**; it's his hours I'd worry about.
do: Plan for Marco dropping to **three days** by sixty-two.
Save **more now** while we have two wages.
Learn Grace's **sow records app** once it runs smoothly.
feel: **Anxious**, a low steady kind, checking **the budget** more.
S1.quote: My husband Marco has done the same tax forms for thirty years, and he'd rather lose a finger than a client.
fieldNote: Her own job feels safe; the anxiety is about **household income**.
The **bank closure** taught her how fast desk jobs go.
She protects **savings first**, cutting the second car instead.

steps.text: Plan with Marco for him going down to three days by sixty-two
Put more into savings while both wages come in
Learn Grace's sow records app once it's running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Marco's job would be gone first, in 2028. Then mine around 2031, when I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to act, not to save every job but to give people time. A bridging payment for older workers, sensible stuff. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, even online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd expect both of us out within three years. AGI does Marco's whole job in 2028, no question. Then robots in 2031 can count piglets and clean pens, and I'm the junior at Millbrook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sell the second car and the caravan, and put it all in savings. I'd ask Grace straight out whether she'd keep me on past the robots. I'd talk to Marco about taking his pension early in 2028, even reduced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It would keep me up. Not hungry-alarmed, but my whole retirement plan would be in pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the three years between Marco's job going and the robots arriving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would be at home, which he'd hate, and I'd be the one earning. I'd want to hold on at Millbrook as long as possible. For three years I'd be the only one in the house with a job, and the job would be piglets, which is the last thing I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got a strong cushion. Why lose sleep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the cushion was meant for when we're seventy, not for six years with no wages. And because I've lived through a job vanishing once. You don't forget how fast it goes.

say: This is **too fast**, and the government must give people time.
Older workers need a **bridging payment**, nothing radical.
think: Robots in **2031** take mine, since I'm the junior at Millbrook.
do: Sell the **second car** and the **caravan**, and save it all.
Ask Grace straight out about **keeping me on**.
Discuss Marco taking an **early pension** in 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over a **broken retirement plan**.
S2.quote: For three years I'd be the only one in the house with a job, and the job would be piglets, which is the last thing I expected.
fieldNote: Both household jobs ending **three years apart** drives her alarm.
She expects to be the **sole earner** briefly, which surprises her.
Her cushion was meant for **later life**, not years without wages.

steps.text: Sell the second car and the caravan and bank the money
Put the car and caravan money straight into savings
Help Marco take his accountant's pension early in 2028
Ask Grace whether she'd keep a hand on once robots come

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, so 2031 for the thinking AI. Marco would be sixty-five, right at his retirement. And robots in 2034, when I'm sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast but manageable, and older workers need a bit of protection. I'd say companies should give notice. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, we'd scrape through. Marco's firm would shrink before 2031, so he might go a year early, but that's not a disaster. My job lasts till I'd planned to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving hard for the next five years. I'd keep working at Millbrook as normal. I'd help Marco look at doing some tax help for neighbours, cash in hand, if his firm cut him early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More watchful than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Giulia and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Luca to keep learning the new tools at his engineering firm. Giulia's a vet nurse, which is hands-on, so I'd tell her she has more time than most. A vet nurse holding a frightened dog is safer from AI than an accountant with a spreadsheet, and I've got one of each at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change how you'd feel about Millbrook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. In the fast one I'd be clinging on. Here I'd just do my last years with the sows and leave on my own terms.

say: It's **fast but manageable** with some protection for older workers.
Companies should give **proper notice** before cutting staff.
think: Marco might go **a year early**, which isn't a disaster.
My job lasts **until I'd planned** to stop anyway.
do: Help Marco do **neighbours' tax help** if cut early.
S3.quote: A vet nurse holding a frightened dog is safer from AI than an accountant with a spreadsheet, and I've got one of each at home.
fieldNote: Five years lines both jobs up with **retirement dates**.
She sorts her children by **hands-on versus desk** work.
Leaving **on her own terms** matters to her after the bank.

steps.text: Keep saving hard every month for the next five years
Keep working with the sows at Millbrook as normal
Help Marco set up tax help for neighbours if cut early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, 2036 and then 2039. We'd both be retired by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan, and not scare people. I'd say it's the young ones who need help choosing careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us, nothing. Marco retires at sixty-five, I do at sixty-six. It's Luca and Giulia's world, and our grandkids'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Millbrook. Keep the savings plan as it is. Watch how the first few years go before telling the kids anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad of the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the pension, if fewer people are working to pay for it. But we've saved, so we'd manage. I lost a job to a machine once at fifty-four, so I've learned to count the years, not the promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across the three fast pictures, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Marco and I are out at the same time or one after the other. With two years both our wages stop before our pensions start, and with ten years we simply retire.

say: There's **time to plan**, so plan without scaring people.
The **young ones** are the ones who need help choosing their careers.
think: Marco retires at **sixty-five** and I do at sixty-six.
This is **Luca and Giulia's** world, and our grandkids'.
do: Keep the **savings plan** as it is.
**Watch the first years** before advising the kids.
S4.quote: With two years both our wages stop before our pensions start, and with ten years we simply retire.
fieldNote: Ten years puts both household jobs **past retirement**.
Her only remaining worry is **pension funding**.
Her bank experience taught her to **count years**, not trust promises.

steps.text: Keep working at Millbrook until sixty-six
Watch the first few years before advising Luca and Giulia

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marco and I would both lose our jobs years before our pensions. What would help is a bridging payment for people over fifty-eight who lose work to AI or robots, and employers giving a year's notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who've already lost a job to a machine, like me at the bank. We know how it feels. Ask us first next time.

headlineQuote: I lost a job to a machine once at fifty-four, so I've learned to count the years, not the promises.
portrait: A former **bank teller** who moved to a pig and maize farm after her branch closed.
Centre and **steady**, she adopts tools once others have them working.
Her household risk sits mostly with **Marco's accounting job**.
Alarmed in **AGI by 2028**, when both incomes end before their pensions.
With more warning, she **saves hard** and leaves farm work on her own terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and Marco's jobs gone before their pensions.
whatWouldHelp: A **bridging payment** for over fifty-eights who lose work to AI or robots.
